title: The Kalachakra
hookLine: the wheel of time teaching, given to huge crowds as a blessing for peace

cards: A field at the edge of a town is filling up. Monks and nuns in maroon. Farmers who walked in from the hills.
Families with thermoses and blankets, visitors from far away sitting cross-legged in the dust.
In a hall nearby, a few monks lean over a low table, tapping colored sand from thin metal funnels, grain by grain, into a huge circular pattern.
When the teaching begins, the crowd stretches so far back that from the last rows the stage is a speck. Some in that crowd won't follow every word. They came anyway.

teach.b: Kalachakra is Sanskrit: kala, time, and chakra, wheel. The wheel of time. It names a tantra, a long and demanding Vajrayana teaching, and the awakened figure at its center.

Tradition says the Buddha taught it, and that it was kept for generations in a hidden kingdom called Shambhala before it came to India and then to Tibet. The teaching speaks of time on more than one level.
Outer time: the sky, the planets, the turning year; Tibetan calendars have leaned on its reckoning. Inner time: the body, its breath and its rhythms.
And a third, called the other Kalachakra: the practice that sees through both and wakes up inside them. One wheel, seen from the stars, from the body, and from the mind.
Then the crowds. Tantric initiations are traditionally given to committed students, but senior lamas, the Dalai Lama among them, have given the Kalachakra to very large gatherings.

Some who come don't intend to take up the full practice. Teachers describe their being there as receiving a blessing, a seed planted, and the gathering itself as an offering for peace in the world. And the sand.
The mandala the monks build with such care is swept up when the teaching ends, and the colored sand is often poured into running water, carrying the blessing outward.
The wheel of time, made visible, and then let go.

how: The Kalachakra initiation is given by senior lamas, including the Dalai Lama, often to very large gatherings; monks build a sand mandala for it, and some attend as a blessing and an offering for world peace rather than to take up the full practice.

games.q: you're a monk. for days you've tapped colored sand into a perfect mandala for the Kalachakra. the teaching is over. what happens to it?
o: it's glued down and kept in the temple.
it's swept up, and the sand is often poured into running water.
it's cut into pieces for the crowd to take home.
games.why: the mandala is swept away when the teaching ends: the wheel of time, made visible, and then let go.

practice: Bring to mind one place where there is fighting or fear right now, a country in the news, a street, a home you know, and hold it gently, the way you'd hold a cup that's too full.
If you pray, offer a prayer for peace from your own tradition, in words you already know; if you don't, simply hold the wish that this place could know peace, and breathe with it.

wordCard.voice: The Kalachakra. The wheel of time: a Vajrayana teaching on outer, inner and awakened time, given to great crowds as a blessing for peace. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit kālacakra: kāla, time, and cakra, wheel. The wheel of time.

carryVoice: Your line: the wheel of time. Even swept-up sand travels on. Rest well.
